title: Daily cross (Luke 9:18–27)
hookLine: Luke adds one word: take up your cross daily
last: YOU GIVE THEM SOMETHING TO EAT.

lines: THE SAME SAYING, ONE EXTRA WORD.
WHOM SAY THE PEOPLE THAT I AM?
cards: Matthew, Mark and Luke all record the same hard saying: if anyone wants to follow me, let him deny himself and take up his cross.
But Luke's version has one extra word, easy to miss, and once you see it, the whole sentence changes shape. It comes after a quiet moment: Jesus was "alone praying," with only his disciples nearby.
Prayer at a turning point, again. When he finishes, he asks the kind of question you'd ask your closest friends late at night, when the crowd has gone home: "Whom say the people that I am?"

teach.h: WHOM SAY YE? THE CHRIST OF GOD.
teach.b: They report the talk: John the Baptist, back from the dead; Elijah; one of the old prophets. Then: "But whom say ye that I am?" Peter answers: "The Christ of God."
Christ means anointed one, the Messiah, the king Israel hoped for.

teach.h: THE SON OF MAN MUST SUFFER.
teach.b: Jesus tells them not to spread it, and says something nobody expected a Messiah to say: "The Son of man must suffer many things, and be rejected of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be slain, and be raised the third day."
Then, to everyone: "If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me." Daily. In Greek, kath hemeran, day by day.
Matthew and Mark don't have it.

teach.h: ROME'S CROSS: CARRIED BY THE CONDEMNED.
teach.b: In Rome's world, a cross wasn't a symbol. It was how the empire executed rebels and slaves, and the condemned man carried the crossbeam through the streets. Taking up your cross meant walking toward the end.
Matthew and Mark say it like a single great decision; Luke adds daily, and it becomes a thing you pick up again every morning. Christians have heard it both ways at once.

teach.h: TAKE UP HIS CROSS DAILY, AND FOLLOW ME.
teach.b: Some have faced death for their faith. Most have faced the ordinary kind: putting someone else first again today, keeping a promise again today.
"For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: but whosoever will lose his life for my sake, the same shall save it." In Luke, losing your life happens one day at a time.

how: Many Christians speak of "carrying their cross" for the ordinary burdens of daily life, and in many traditions the daily offering of one's day to God is a morning practice.

o: a small cross worn every day as jewelry
the ordinary weight picked up again each day

games.q: what's inside Luke 9:18–27 — tap the pairs.

s: Matthew, Mark and Luke all say "take up his cross daily"
Luke says Jesus was praying before he asked who they said he was
he was alone praying, with his disciples nearby.
in Jesus' day, the cross was already a religious symbol
it was Rome's way of executing people; the condemned carried the crossbeam.

games.q: Jesus asks his closest friends: but who do you say that I am? you're Peter. what do you say?
games.why: Peter says the Christ of God. and Jesus answers that the Son of man must suffer, and that following him means a cross taken up daily.

practice: Think about the ordinary weight that's yours to pick up every day, caring for a parent, a hard job, patience with a child or with your own body, and see it plainly, no bigger and no smaller than it is.
Picture tomorrow morning, picking it up again on purpose, with a little love in it. If you pray, you can offer that daily weight to God; if you don't, simply choose to carry it with care.

wordCard.voice: Daily cross. Peter names Jesus the Christ of God, and Jesus says anyone who follows him must take up the cross, and Luke adds the word daily.

orig.note: Greek: day by day, daily. the word only Luke adds to "take up his cross."

carryVoice: Your line: daily. Not one great moment, but every morning, again. That's day five hundred thirty-five.
